text: Okay. All right. Good afternoon, everyone. I'd like to call this April 6th meeting of the Curriculum and Instruction Committee to order. My name is Dr. Rasheed. I am the chair of this committee. I appreciate you all being here. The purpose of today's meeting is we want to review and approve the minutes from our last meeting, and we have two updates. We got world languages and cultures, and we have the Office of Visual and Performing Arts update as well. We do not have public

comment, and we have no one signed up for that. But we need to approve the minutes from our March 5th meeting. And has everyone had a chance to review the minutes, and are there any corrections or additions? Okay, if no objections or corrections, I entertain a motion to approve the minutes from March 5th. I move to approve the draft minutes of the March 5th, 2026 Curriculum and Instruction meeting. Okay. Thank you, Ms. Chernoff. All right. All those in favor say aye.

Oh, I second. Thank you. Spring break has got to me. So all those in favor say aye. Aye. Aye. And all those opposed, none. So the minutes have been approved. Okay, great. So let's go on to our first agenda item, which is 4.01, Office of World Languages. I will first turn it over to Mr. Slevin. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Rasheed. I'm happy to have Mr. Roundsley and Ms. Kelly James joining us this afternoon to share an update

on what is happening in the world of world languages. So I think Mr. Roundsley is going to start. Good afternoon. So as Mr. Slevin just said, Ms. James and I are going to talk a little bit about what's happening in the world of world languages. And on the next slide, you'll see some of the things that we're hoping to highlight today. First, to look at our enrollment trends and give an update on our offerings around world languages, some exciting additions that we've made and changes.

Second, to explore considerations for expanding world language options, new options, division-wide, and also highlight some really, I think, exciting work that's happening right now around alternative pathways that recognize and build on students' language-- Already students' gifts around languages that they have, and how we are recognizing and supporting that. So Kelly will give some updates on that later. We first wanted to talk about our enrollment trends that we're seeing around world

languages across LCPS. And on the next slide, you'll see a graph of where some of our bigger languages, so Spanish is represented by that purple line, French by the blue line, German green, Latin purple, and American Sign Language is red. Now, that graph on the left shows all the languages, which can be a little bit deceiving because Spanish greatly outpaces all of those other languages. And we have seen a growth in Spanish

division-wide, around a 7% increase in students taking Spanish since the '21/'22 school year up till this year. If you look on the right, that's much more zoomed in because we're talking about much smaller numbers in French, German, Latin, and American Sign Language, and those languages all have seen some declines. Latin especially has seen a more significant decline, as has American Sign Language. But I think

something we're excited about is you see a small growth in American Sign Language for this year. Partly that's because of the centralized staffing in the World Language office that the board approved for this year. There was two new American Sign Language positions that were created that have been used to start programs at schools that didn't have American Sign Language positions to start with. And we are seeing some growth for this year and also continuing growth into next year, which has been a really exciting

development that we've seen in the support for being able to offer smaller programs without taking away from a school's staffing as well. On the next slide, you'll see languages by school and the enrollment of languages by school. And again, I think across the board, you can see that Spanish is by far, that purple line, the most enrolled language across the division. But I think you also see here really some pockets of other languages that are

an important part of communities, really have teachers who are committed to building and recruiting and retaining students in their languages. So if you look at, say, John Champ's French program or Stonebridge's French program, there's lots of strong growth there. Or Freedom's German program, or those red blocks that represent American Sign Languages with teachers who have been really committed in growing their programs, where we see multiple teachers teaching those classes. So we see really strong--

In everywhere, we see these languages represented, maybe not in every school, but when we have teachers who are really dedicated to building and supporting these programs and recruiting and retaining students in those programs, we see really good strength in them as well. The right column shows middle school just quickly, and again, these are the feeder programs into some of those other programs. At the high school level, again, Spanish is by far the language that most students are enrolled in. And Kelly, a little bit later, is going to talk about the

languages that we offer in middle school that feed into these as well. But across the board, you see strong numbers for students taking world languages at the middle school level, and strong feeder programs building on each other between middle and high school. This is a theme we'll return to a little bit later when we talk about the visual and performing arts as well. So getting into our course offerings and our course

progressions. So students can start learning a world language in seventh grade. Many of the languages are available through six levels ... which is the six years often an AP level course. Some of our high schools are able to offer dual enrollment courses if the teacher is certified to teach that, and that's usually the fifth year of the language. And students who are native or heritage speakers of Spanish can opt for Spanish for fluent speakers, which progresses through a level four, which is an honors course.

So as we look to expand our world language course offerings, this chart shows a comparison of districts and the world languages that are available to students in person at the middle and the high school levels. The bold languages in red are the less commonly taught languages that are a little bit more difficult to staff. In LCPS, Arabic is currently offered at one school. It's our pilot year of offering that. Mandarin is at two schools, and Russian is offered at one high school.

So as we look to support and expand world languages, we're really excited to offer a new course at the middle school next year, that's going to be your year-long course called Exploratory Languages, which will build exposure to all language opportunities, giving students a little bit of a taste if they are not ready to commit to one language or if they're unsure of what language they do want to take in high school. We're also using centralized staffing to support languages. As Mr. Ounsley shared,

we already saw a growth in ASL from those centralized staffing positions and being able to start programs and sustain those through centralized staffing. Of course, strengthening curriculum development and consistency and collaborating with HRTD, and school leadership to support and staff those smaller programs. So when we're considering expanding world language offerings, there's three things that we really need to keep in mind, that's interest, location, and resources.

So it's really important to have a demonstrated community interest in a potential new language. This includes not only enrollment demand, but also meaningful engagement with families and community stakeholders to understand the cultural connections, student motivation, and long-term program viability. So we have some data from a 2022 survey that indicated a very strong interest from students in Japanese, Korean, and Arabic. So this strong interest ensures that programs are not only just launched

successfully, but they're sustained in time with consistent enrollment and support. We want to ensure that these expansion opportunities incorporate workplace readiness skills. So an example of that is that we do plan to pilot a Spanish for Healthcare Workers course. We're going to start piloting that at our hand size schools and look to expand to other schools as there's interest in that. Going on to locations, expanding offering requires a strategic

approach to placement so that students access diverse language programs is equitable for students in different regions of LCPS. So that includes balancing new programs with existing ones, avoiding over-concentration of certain languages in specific areas, and ensuring that students across the county have reasonable access to a variety of language learning opportunities. And then finally, it's also about having strong resource and the availability of those resources.

A big part of that is recruiting and retaining highly qualified teachers with both linguistic and pedagogical expertise in the target language, which is particularly challenging in the less commonly taught languages. And by also ensuring that we have the teachers to sustain up through multiple levels. Partnership with HRTD is essential for recruiting these hard-to-staff languages, and we have to have high-quality standards aligned instructional materials that support proficiency-based learning and

reflect authentic cultural perspectives. There's also partnerships in the community and potential grant funding that could help to offset some of the startup costs for expanding new languages in LCPS. So as we talk about some alternative pathways to world language credits, we have done a lot of work in this area over the past year. A little bit of a background on world language credit through testing.

It's a way for students who have a background in a world language, who speak another language at home or learned it elsewhere, to earn a high school credit in that language, which could fulfill the advanced diploma requirement and potentially meet the requirement for the Virginia Department of Education Seal of Biliteracy at graduation. So previously, we had offered credit through testing in 28 languages, which is

a good list, but by no means fully representing all of the languages that are spoken in LCPS. So we went from offering credit through testing in 28 languages to 130 by working with an external partner. Working with a third-party service for this assessment also expedited the receiving of results of our assessment, which allowed us to provide a second testing window.

So we have a fall testing window and then a spring testing window. We have six different dates in the fall, and we had six different dates in the spring. This was the first year that we were able to do a spring testing. And we offer the locations at six different high schools across the county to provide access for students so they're not having to drive necessarily all the way across the county. We try to ensure one testing location in the fall and a different testing location

in the spring at our Leesburg schools, our schools out west, our schools in the east, and our schools in Dulles South. So that all areas of the county are represented, and so students have an opportunity for that. So, we had 130 languages that were available to students, and these are the new languages that were assessed in the fall and in the spring of 2026So going on, this is a history of our students who have registered for credit through

testing. This year, having two windows provided a huge record-breaking number of students who took advantage of this opportunity, and we're really excited, especially since this is just the first year that we were able to offer spring testing. We still have some families who don't necessarily know. Again, it's a slow process of getting this out to our families who don't necessarily know that we now offer the assessment in the language that they speak, or as we only just recently added our languages.

Going on to talk about the Seal of Biliteracy, which is one of the other benefits of credit through testing. The Seal of Biliteracy is an award from the Virginia Department of Education to recognize a student who has attained proficiency in English and one or more world languages by high school graduation. So the seal serves to certify attainment of biliteracy for students, employers, and institutions of higher education. It's a statement of accomplishment that helps signal evidence of a student's readiness for career, college, and engagement as a global citizen.

And as of July 1st of 2025, Virginia House Bill 2360 became law, which designated the Virginia Seal of Biliteracy as a workplace readiness high-demand industry credential. So we're really excited. That's a really great news for students who are earning that. This next chart shows the number of Seals of Biliteracy that were awarded over the past five years. It's important to note that this includes students who are seniors that year

only. So while we have the second line indicate students who earned that through the process that we have through LCPS, there are other ways that they can earn the Seal of Biliteracy. A lot of students earn the seal through an AP language exam, or if their school has a separate assessment that's approved by the Virginia Department of Education, they're able to run that at the school level. And we have students who are earning the seal that way. Great news for us is that of the 387 seniors who have

earned the Seal of Biliteracy just this year, that's only for our fall testing as we just completed our spring testing in March, and so we're still getting our results back there. But 39 of the 387 students who earned the seal so far are in 11 of the new languages that are offered. So that's really exciting for us that we have senior students who previously weren't offered that opportunity are taking advantage of that opportunity and they have that. So I am anticipating awarding over 800 Seals of Biliteracy

in LCPS this spring just for the seniors. I'm happy to answer any questions you have. Thank you so much for that presentation. I have some questions. Well, just before we move on, I did see with that graph chart, I think it's Mr. Ramsey, you had mentioned that there were two new ASL positions. I just wanted to know where and if that correlated with the graph at all.

In ASL, our programs this year are at... We have a program at Briarwoods, Rock Ridge, Potomac Falls, and Park View. And all of those programs started with an ASL One this year, and we'll be adding ASL Two next year. So we will be further increasing those numbers. Great. Yeah. One of those schools had actually two classes of ASL One. So they had the numbers in two requested. That course was worth two classes.

Great. Yeah, I know. It kind of goes with if you build it, they will come type of thing. But yeah, thank you for that. I just wanted to know how many students take advantage of the CTT per year. I think you already said it- Yes ... but I just wanted to see. So we have on sixteenth, is that those are the numbers of students who register. They register themselves through a portal online. To sign up, they pick their date, their language, their location.

Okay. And how are students informed or families informed about the opportunity to earn the CTT? So previously, we had primarily communicated through world language teachers through that, but a lot of the students who need to take advantage of the opportunity might not be enrolled in a world language. We have a lot of EL students who would need to take advantage of this opportunity, and they're not necessarily in a language. So we have made it a priority to work with communications.

It was in the LCPS newsletter. We also partnered with the EL department. We had a presentation at the FACE Empowered Conference for families and students that was on a Saturday in the fall to inform families about this opportunity. We have presented at those FACE-- It was like a I don't know what it was called.

The Family Room. Yes. So we presented the Family Room so that our families are made aware of this since that's a big percentage of the students who would be taking advantage of this opportunity. Also partnering with school counseling so that the counselors are aware of this opportunity to inform their students whether it is in meeting for course selection for following year, so that they know that this opportunity is coming up.

Awesome. And are they informed of the barriers? Like what could be the cost, or is there a registration fee along with it? So students are able to take this assessment twice over the course of their high school career. They can only take it in high school grades nine through twelve. They can take it once per academic year. So if a student tested in the fall, they were unable to test in the spring, but they can test again next year. And it is free of cost to students. Oh, awesome. And

what percentage of students who take the exam successfully earn the credits? I don't know if we have data on that. So we are in the process of collecting that as we get our results back. I would say that, I don't have-- We can get you the specific number, but they can earn, depending upon their proficiency level. It's not like a pass-fail test. Oh. It gives them a proficiency level. Depending upon their proficiency score, they can earn one, two, or three world language credits.

And are we exploring any avenues or pathways so that students can take advantage of CTT at the current moment? I know we've exhausted quite a lot of measures, but we're heightening awareness through all the- Mm-hmm ... pathways you had mentioned. But is there any other that we're possibly exploring? I can't think of any, because you really covered it all, but I was just curious about it. I'm always open to new ideas. At this time, we're looking at ways to expand this and to make sure that all of the students who need to take advantage of this

opportunity are provided a way to do so. All right. Thank you so much. If I could just add to that. I think that this year also is a significant expansion of CTT. As Kelly mentioned in her presentation, we did go with a third-party vendor this year that does the testing for us, which really enables us to go faster, to test more students, and the tests are more rigorous. There's now a speaking portion of the test that wasn't on there before. We had a

local process that we used that required recruiting and hiring community members to read and score these exams. We're now going with a national vendor who does this in other local school divisions. Which really, students were waiting a long time to get their results. The results now come back in a week or so. Some of the more commonly spoken languages, like Spanish, we get Spanish results in a matter of three or four days, and their results are automatically uploaded, so they can see how they did.

But we had all of our testing was complete, I think all of the results were back within six weeks in the fall window. So, we do believe this is the first year of doing it this way, and this will continue to grow as well, because we have seen some strong growth, and I think the process is much more streamlined for families to participate than it had been previously. So exciting. I'll now turn it over to my colleagues. Any questions? Yes, Ms. Sherwood.

Thank you, Dr. Rasheed. Thank you, Ms. James, for being here. I feel like you've become a frequent flyer, and I'm enjoying it. My questions do honestly kind of surround around some of those other programs. So a couple of just logistical questions. One is for the new middle school course that's more of an exploration. Is that starting in seventh grade? Would that be offered in seventh? Seventh or eighth. Seventh or eighth? Okay. And then what is the requirement for students with languages? Is it three years or four?

For the Virginia advanced diploma, it is three years to earn- Okay ... an advanced diploma. Okay. So if you- Or two years of two different languages. Oh. Yes. Okay. They have two options. So if you choose to do the exploration year in seventh instead of starting your language- Mm-hmm ... it would potentially delay your elective choice ability down the road. Yes. Okay. Potentially. Okay. But if they're not sure what language they want to take, or

if they are not quite ready to commit to learning a high school credit-bearing course in middle school, this would be a great option for them. Yeah, I love that we're doing it. I think we need more of these kinds of things in middle school. I think it's a great way to expand these programs and to get kids on the right track to where they need to go. We had the Wheel. I'm dating myself, but we did the Wheel in Fairfax County when I was in school, and that's how I ended up choosing Spanish. So I think it's a great option. I'm glad to see it kind of making its way

back into our public schools. And then my question really, and you probably don't have this data offhand, but maybe another time. Do we have the data on once kids have met those three-year requirements, what the drop-off is then? Like, are kids continuing? I would love to see what that looks like. Because a lot of this sometimes feels like kids are doing the requirement, and then they're moving on to other electives. And the reason I ask is we're really shifting gears

here to a pathways-based, program-based model in LCPS. And so if we're going to be doing that, and we are going to be compete, it feel, and we're going to have this conversation with fine arts, too, so I'm queuing you up. But it feels like there's so much competition for electives. So when I hear you say, "We need community buy-in, we need the teachers, we need to think of all of those things," don't we also have to think about what it's competing against in order to make sure that these

programs are sustainable? That may be more of a Mr. Slevin question. Yes. But I think it's a question for all of us across the board within the content areas, being thoughtful about what we're putting in front of our schools and the program of studies. But that's definitely on our mind, and it's part of the conversation we're having internally about what is impacting these numbers, and are they actually competing? Yeah.

Because we are looking at these in slices. We'll look at fine arts enrollment next, but when you compare them all, there are a number of factors that are influencing it besides just them eating each other and competing. Yeah. In isolation, I want all these things, right? And I want DLI, and I want fine arts, and I want all the things. But we have to recognize that the student's time is limited, and the electives are getting thinner and thinner, it feels, with these programs.

So I just want to be mindful, and that leads to my last question, which is, I guess because DLI has advanced now through third grade, so parents, I think, are starting to think about it going to middle school, and we had the meeting, and then there was an article about it. So I think we've been getting ... emails in our inbox, support for DLI in middle school. I know you talked about we're starting to noodle on that a little bit, but DLI does not count as

a language credit. How do those two overlap, or do they? So as it is right now, it wouldn't count as a high school credit-bearing world language- Okay ... language class. Yeah. Okay. So they'd still have to do the full track. Once they got into middle school, they'd still have to do the regular language courses? That would be, again, depending upon the middle school model. If we go into middle school, that would be dependent upon the middle school model that we

choose. But there are ways for them to earn world language credit in middle school through DLI courses. Okay. Yes. Well, hats off to you all. This is a lot to manage. There's a lot of moving parts, and I'm really excited about the credit through testing. I know we had that presentation last year, and it was so exciting to see what that third vendor offered in terms of us being able to expand. Clearly, it's expanding. So that's really exciting, especially for our English language learners. Very impressive. Really excited to see how the middle school stuff goes and appreciate the work. Thank you.

Thank you, Ms. Chernov. Any other questions? Yes, Mr. Svenson. Thank you, Dr. Rashid. The credit to testing program is great. This is really exciting to see the numbers on the charts here. I had a couple questions about the offerings for Arabic, Mandarin. I know that we're offering that at the Academy of Global Linguistic Studies, and was wondering for the model currently, is

that taught at particular high schools, outside of AGLS? Are there particular high schools that are offering that, and what's the plan to expand those offerings? Because when you look at this, it does strike you as it's a little old school, the languages that are still taught in LCPS, and it's great that we're expanding and curious about what the plan is going forward. So the two schools where we have Mandarin currently are not our AGLS, as AGLS is going to be starting next year. And the Arabic school is also a

different school. And as we are looking at next year, there are other high schools who have indicated interest in course requests to offer Arabic, so we're looking at Arabic expanding to additional high schools beyond our pilot school and our AGLS host school next year as well. And is that the same for Russian? Because I saw Russian on the chart as well. And I guess to follow up on that, about Arabic, Mandarin, and Russian, and maybe you don't have on hand the particular schools, but are

they all taught at different schools? Yeah. Or are those programs- Those are all different schools ... housed at the same? Yes. They're all at different schools. Thank you. Yeah, I think that would be great to expand those offerings further, in addition to AGLS, but continuing for the general population of students. And I also was curious, this is also a question I had about the visual and performing art slides,

but do you all have data for before the last five years to compare the enrollment in world languages pre- and post-COVID? Just because I was curious, I see the starting point for the graphs is post-COVID, and I was curious if there was a drop-off or not of these electives and what the impact has been in terms of getting folks back enrolled in these.

Thank you. Appreciate it. Thank you, Mr. Svenson, and thank you for answering the questions. All right. We will now move on to our next item, 4.02, update of Office of Visual and Performing Arts. I will move it over to Mr. Rounsley. Thank you. So we are going to follow the same model with the visual and performing arts that we just did in talking about world languages. And so on the next slide, we have a few of the

key outcomes that we'd like to talk about today, same as we did with world languages, to talk about enrollment data for the visual and performing arts across our secondary schools. Also try to understand a little bit around why we're seeing some of these trends and the factors that shape them. And Mr. Pearson, who is down here, our visual and performing arts supervisor, will share some division-level actions that we are taking to strengthen our visual and performing arts programs and discuss potential enhancements to support the

co-curricular aspects of the visual and performing arts. So just as we did with world languages, we'll start with some enrollment trends across the three big areas of the visual and performing arts, which are band, art, and theater. We do see a rise in the enrollments of students in our music programs from 2021 to 2022. There is a sharper decline in art, and there's a slight decline in theater arts, but one of the things

that's really important to recognize with these slides, to add a little context, is that unlike some other content areas, the visual performing arts has a rich co-curricular aspects as well. These are students enrolled in these classes. Our count is that somewhere around 4,000 students are actually enrolled in theater arts because they participate outside of school. They're not enrolling in the electives. As Ms. Chernov noted, there is steep competition for many of those electives, but

they are invested and part of the programs, it's just not reflected in our course enrollment data. The next slide, again, shows our programs across our schools. And once again, you see the pockets of some real strengths where these programs are invested in a part of our communities. If you look at some of the theater programs, you'll notice very large numbers of students enrolled in some theater programs. And again, Mr. Pearson is going to speak to this, but I think that speaks

to the relationships that teachers build with students, the sense of belonging that we create in these programs, the sense of community and tradition that are part of these programs. And so while not every school has strong programs across the board, we do see a lot of strength in the visual and performing arts in some of our programs everywhere. On the right-hand side, you'll see our middle schoolsIt's important to note there, if you look at Willard Middle School, there's over 2,000 students enrolled, which there are not 2,000 students enrolled at Willard Middle School.

But the reason why is because in the middle school, in sixth grade, every student takes art and every student takes music. So there is a double count of our sixth-grade students in those classes. But once again, we take a lot of steps to make sure students do have broad exposure to the visual and performing arts in middle school, and some of those same themes that we just talked about in world languages around strong collaborative feeder patterns and working together and recruitment efforts across the middle and high school will come into play as well to keep those programs growing.

For example, at Willard Middle School, it feeds into Light Ridge. And while those are both large schools, I know there's a strong collaborative bond between those two schools and working together to keep students enrolled and invested in these programs. The next slide shows the growth over the last five years of different visual and performing arts programs at each of our high schools. And I think something worth noting here is that we do have some schools that are seeing really strong growth in the visual and performing

arts. If you look at Parkview, Light Ridge is a new school, which explains that very large growth. But if you look at a school like Parkview or Riverside or Stonebridge, you see continuing growth in the visual and performing arts programs. And I think what this highlights is that our teachers are doing some really great things to keep students involved and invested in this, that there is a lot of expertise in the room to talk about how we keep students involved and invested in these programs. And while this

is all visual performing arts, it doesn't go to the nuance of art versus music. We are seeing places where we have strong growth, and our teachers are really leading the way in helping to recruit and keep students as part of these programs. I'm going to turn it over to Mr. Pearson, who's going to talk about the support that his office provides in making that happen, and some of the things that we are seeing schools do to help build on that success. Thank you, Jeff. Of course, the first part of that support is being aware of what's

out there, situational awareness, lots of conversations over the years, 18 years for me in this position, and knowing what's happened on the ground level. There's so many factors that come together. But on this slide here, we've identified just a few challenges and success factors that keep coming up. Amongst those are, already referenced this evening, the competition that's created through additional electives as we keep adding things to the plate to provide opportunities for students.

And there's only so much room in the schedule that they can add, so they're having to make tough choices sometimes. We do hear feedback from our, especially at the secondary level, that once students finish their two credits in the arts, then there's pressure to move into other courses and things. And so we do lose students to that and to early release. If the band class is scheduled in the afternoon, those students aren't in that program anymore as a result.

Probably the biggest thing here, we talk about staffing, the FTE, and how those are utilized. We've referenced previously there's sometimes a philosophical component. Decisions have to be made at the school level that have impacts. But if we pull back FTE, let's say from the art program, without a change in the enrollment, we will see a drop in enrollment because there are fewer courses offered by default. At the same time, when we have a program at a school that only has

one art teacher, it's hard for us to offer all of the offerings that we have available in the program of studies. So maybe that school can't offer ceramics because there's not somebody there to teach it. So those are challenges. There's a reason the VPA office support is in the middle, because we try to bridge those problems and provide supports. I will come back to that. The success factors include, and again, it was mentioned earlier, there is research that shows that one of the strongest

indicators or factors in a student staying engaged in these programs is their connection with their teacher. And so that's hugely a part. When that culture's built, you spend a lot of time out of school, especially in the music program, in theater. So there's kind of a bond and family that's built there that keeps students in the program. Again, we referenced earlier where we have the ability for, let's say, the high school orchestra teacher to come down occasionally and

engage with the eighth graders at the high school level or at the middle school level, get to know them, that increases the chance that those students are going to stay engaged in that program. So again, personal connections. And of course, there's the broader thing. We see this happen where there's a sense of pride, not just in the school, but in the broader community, that they're proud of the programs that they have, and when we have that, it kind of feeds on itself in the whole entire community.

In between, when we become aware of issues, we stay in contact with our teachers. We are open to administrators. Over the years, I've offered on many occasions guidance to administrators, encouragement to offer programs. I recall one instance when we were opening a new high school program. Orchestra program was getting off the ground. It was still small at the time. But the decision was or the question was, are we going to offer an orchestra

block for these students? Well, if we didn't, that meant the students that were pulling from the previous high school as they opened the new high school were not going to have that opportunity. So it took a while, but that school eventually, before it was all said and done, offered one block of orchestra, and now it's a full-fledged, very successful program. So we intersect at various points along the line and remain available.

So I want to go into the support we provide for courses and programs, especially on the financial end. I want to thank the school board, most grateful to each of you for the incredible support you've provided us over the years, but certainly this year, and it seems like it wasn't that long ago, I was sitting here talking about proposing, telling you what we needed with allotments, and to see that come to fruition, I'm most grateful. We all are, and we're very excited. We do recognize with the model that we use, especially for the music
